feed.title: JanusPath
feed.subtitle: JanusPath is a workshop for structural insight across philosophy, society, technology, and literature—seeking clarity and actionable paths through complexity and noise.

entry.title: Modeling Thought Through Language: EchoPath Labs Is My First Step
entry.summary: My long-term goal is to model how people think through the words they express. EchoPath Labs is my first step, connecting meaning, bounded action, and cognitive history in engineering collaboration so that interpretations can be tested and revised through practice.

entry.title: Why Multiple Agents, Rather Than One Universal Harness
entry.summary: A model fitting into a harness does not mean the resulting agent is trustworthy. This essay explains why a calibrated Harness + Model should be treated as a complete Agent Profile, and how RelayPact enables a trusted Host Agent to delegate bounded work to other agents.

entry.title: Rejection Is Easy; Reconstruction Is Hard
entry.summary: Rejecting an old structure creates direction, enemies, and consensus. Real reconstruction requires understanding why it formed, what it still does, and which deeper conditions keep reproducing its failures.

entry.title: Seeing the World Through Structuralism: Before Judging People, Look at the Structure
entry.summary: Why do organizations keep selecting the same kinds of people even after leaders change? A practical structuralist lens reveals the systems shaping behavior.

entry.title: Agents Don't Need Org Charts; They Need Context Boundaries
entry.summary: Multi-agent systems may need clear boundaries around knowledge, state, permissions, tools, and decisions more than human-style job titles. Agents are replaceable; context is durable.

entry.title: Software Organizations in the AI Era: From Multi-Person Teams to One-Person Organizations
entry.summary: AI may reshape software development less by accelerating coding than by changing how work is organized. Explore the shift toward human-governed, agent-executed teams.

entry.title: The Stronger the Agent, the More We Need Software Engineering
entry.summary: AI makes code cheaper, not complexity free. Architecture, modularity, schemas, tests, and domain models reduce agent uncertainty through cognitive reuse.

entry.title: Rethinking Password Management in the Agent Era
entry.summary: As AI agents act across GitHub, APIs, and cloud platforms, KeptNear's Local Broker shows how to authorize credential-backed capabilities without exposing raw secrets.

entry.title: When AI Begins to Think Along Your Lines
entry.summary: When ChatGPT does more than remember preferences and begins extending a person's structure of thought, the central challenge of human-AI collaboration shifts from storing more information to sustaining a cognitive subject that is still changing.

entry.title: Why I Started Simplifying My AI Agents
entry.summary: After intensive use of AI agents such as Codex and Claude Code, I began removing unnecessary skills, rules, and context. This article explains why more configuration is not always better and how restraint can make agents more reliable.

entry.title: What You See Is Not the Problem Itself, but the Way It Becomes Visible
entry.summary: An accessible introduction to JanusPath's movement from structural reflection to origin-observation reflection: complex problems concern not only content and structure, but also how observation begins.

entry.title: From Writing Code to Governing Agents: Software Engineering's New Question in the AI Era
entry.summary: As AI agents increasingly generate code, the engineer's core value is shifting toward extracting rules, designing constraints, maintaining context, and governing agents. The new production object of software engineering is executable experience, rules, and cognitive assets.

entry.title: A Team SOP for Using Codex, OpenSpec, and Superpowers
entry.summary: A team-oriented Codex usage SOP covering OpenSpec, Superpowers, context preservation, requirements discovery, product planning, implementation, validation, operations analysis, troubleshooting, and knowledge handoff.

entry.title: Team Atmosphere Is Not Culture; It Is Noise Management
entry.summary: Team atmosphere is shaped less by cultural slogans than by how leaders handle noise, deviation, and uncertainty. Beginning with an argument over an early food delivery, this article explains defensive work, degradation spirals, risk tiers, tolerance bands, and practical noise budgets.

entry.title: AI Agents Are Powerful, but They Drift
entry.summary: AI agents perform exceptionally well on short tasks, yet often suffer from semantic drift in long-running workflows. This article distinguishes context windows from persistent memory and argues that today's agents cannot reliably preserve system structure, leaving structural sovereignty in human hands.

entry.title: If Humans Stop Writing Code, AI Will Get Worse Too
entry.summary: If most future code is generated by AI, models will increasingly learn from code written by other models. Small errors and poor structures may be copied until they harden into convention, degrading quality and contributing to model collapse. What improves a system is still human judgment about boundaries, trade-offs, and structure.

entry.title: Structural Noise
entry.summary: During the city's Eighth-Round Order Optimization, an algorithmic ethics reviewer is classified as an unpredictable “structural noise point.” As identity, social access, and resources are stripped away layer by layer, he uses a performance of absolute loyalty to make the system downgrade itself and prise loose the anchor of its rules.

entry.title: Inversion of Control Through a Structuralist Lens
entry.summary: This article steps away from implementation details to reinterpret Inversion of Control through structuralism. A dependency is fundamentally a power relationship, and IoC externalizes the right to decide. This lens connects dependency injection, configuration, low-code systems, and system evolution.

entry.title: Software Engineering Is Full of Hidden Thinking Models
entry.summary: Software engineering is never purely technical. It is a practical exercise in structural thinking. Through modularity, architecture, debugging, and iteration, engineers have long practiced an unnamed philosophy.

entry.title: Why Does Philosophy Always Seem to Belong to Elites?
entry.summary: Why does philosophy feel so inaccessible? By examining linguistic barriers, institutional divisions of labor, and structural silence, this article argues that philosophy is “elitized” when the right to ask fundamental questions is unevenly distributed.
